title: EMFormer: Forecasting the Far Future Without Forgetting the Recent
one_liner: A weather model learns to predict months ahead by training on both short- and long-term patterns together, so it does not unlearn what works for now to chase what works later.
lead: Weather forecasting is hard because a model trained to predict far into the future often forgets how to predict the next day well — like a student cramming for an exam next month but bombing today's quiz. This paper introduces EMFormer, a transformer (a model that attends to many past patterns at once) that learns both short and long forecasts in one go, using a clever training recipe that keeps both skills sharp.

paras: Weather forecasters face a dilemma. To predict what will happen in 30 days, a model needs to learn long-range patterns — big pressure systems that take weeks to form. But those patterns are rare in the training data, buried under daily noise. So trainers add special loss functions that reward predicting far ahead.

Here is what breaks: the moment you start rewarding distant predictions, the model stops learning short-range weather. It unlearns the daily skills it mastered before. This is catastrophic forgetting — the model forgets its old training to chase the new goal. At the same time, predicting 30 days out means 30 chances to make a mistake; each wrong prediction ripples forward, compounding into nonsense. And training the model from scratch each time takes weeks of compute.

callout.html: EMFormer trains on both short and long forecasts at the same time with a smart loss function, keeping both skills sharp while using a single efficient local pattern detector instead of expensive full-grid pattern-matching.

panels.title: 5. Result: Sharp Forecasts at All Ranges

steps.text: One convolution kernel reads the weather grid at multiple scales (coarse and fine details together).
Keep training examples that span both short (24 hours) and long (weeks) prediction windows in the same batch.
A smooth wave function automatically shifts emphasis: early in training, focus on short range; mid-training, balance both; late training, emphasize long range.
The transformer attends to patterns that matter for both timescales, so neither is forgotten.
One forward pass outputs predictions for day 1, day 7, day 14, and day 30 all at once, with shared learned skills.

paras: The paper changes two things at once: the model's backbone (how it reads the input weather grid) and the training process (which forecasts to reward). Instead of an expensive transformer that attends to every pixel of every historical day, EMFormer uses a single convolution to capture patterns at multiple scales — coarse (the big fronts) and fine (the local storms) in one forward pass. Then, during training, it uses a composite loss that smoothly swaps emphasis between short and long forecast goals over the course of learning.

hidden.name: Prediction stability across forecast horizons
paras: Temporal consistency is a measure of how well a model's prediction for day 30 stays coherent with its prediction for day 1 — not contradicting itself, not suddenly forgetting local patterns when zooming out to the month view. EMFormer measures this by comparing the accuracy of short forecasts before and after training on long forecasts.

The paper estimates it by tracking the accuracy of the 24-hour forecast on the same weather grids, both before finetuning and after finetuning for the 30-day horizon. If the short-range accuracy drops by 5 percent, consistency is poor. If it stays stable (within 1-2 percent), the model has learned to keep both skills.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger after EMFormer. The short-range accuracy and extreme-event recall stay high (marked).

reads.html: Temporal consistency means the model's different forecasts do not contradict each other. A good weather model predicts tomorrow's high temperature the same way whether it is asked just for tomorrow or for tomorrow-through-month-end.
Measured as short-horizon accuracy retention after long-horizon finetuning, and as the Pearson correlation between 1-step and 30-step predictions on the same grid cells.

mechanism.h2: Why Sinusoidal Weighting Keeps Both Skills
paras: The core idea is that the model learns in stages: first, nail the obvious daily patterns (because they have lots of examples); then, carefully layer in the rare long-range patterns (because adding them too fast drowns out short-range learning). A sinusoidal function — a smooth wave that goes up, then down, then up again — automatically manages this. Early in training, the weight on short-range loss is high (the model focuses on day 1); mid-way through, both short and long get equal weight; late in training, long-range gets the emphasis to squeeze out every percent of improvement.

Why does this work? Because when a task shift is gradual (not sudden), the model's shared pattern detectors have time to reorganize. A weight that predicts day 1 starts as a general feature detector (this looks like a cold front). As training gradually shifts emphasis, that detector refines itself to work in both contexts — predicting where the front goes in 24 hours AND in 30 days. If you switched the emphasis suddenly, the weight would be torn between two contradictory goals and forget both. The smooth sine curve prevents the tear.

stages.s: Weather grid: pixels, time steps, variables (pressure, temperature, wind)
Single-pass multi-scale convolution: coarse and fine features at once
Transformer attends to patterns that predict both short and long horizons
Sinusoidal loss weighting: smoothly shifts focus across training epochs
Predictions: day 1, day 7, day 14, day 30 — all accurate, none forgotten

math.words: Total loss equals short-range loss times a weight that starts high, then dips low, plus long-range loss times a weight that starts low, then rises high; the weights are a smooth wave that oscillates.
math.equation: L_total = w_short(t) * L_short + w_long(t) * L_long, where w_short(t) = (1 + cos(pi * t / T)) / 2 and w_long(t) = 1 - w_short(t)
symbols: error in predicting the next 24 hours on test grids
weight on short-range loss; 1.0 at start, 0.0 at midpoint, back to 1.0 at end
weight on long-range loss; starts 0, rises to 1.0 at midpoint

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Epoch 0 (start): w_short = 1.0, w_long = 0.0. If L_short = 10 and L_long = 50, then L_total = 1.0 * 10 + 0.0 * 50 = 10.
Epoch 50 (middle): w_short = 0.0, w_long = 1.0. Same losses, but L_total = 0.0 * 10 + 1.0 * 50 = 50. The model now learns long-range.
Epoch 100 (end): w_short = 1.0, w_long = 0.0 again. L_total = 1.0 * 10 + 0.0 * 50 = 10. Back to short-range focus to polish.
Result: By epoch 100, both L_short and L_long are much lower (say 3 and 8) because the model learned both. L_total spirals downward, never gets stuck optimizing one at the cost of the other.

math.note: The sine curve works because by giving each forecast horizon a turn, the model's shared pattern detectors (its weights) have time to adapt smoothly instead of being torn between two opposing goals. Early layers learn "is this a cold front" (useful for both); later layers refine that answer for each timescale separately.

bars.h2: How Short-Range and Long-Range Accuracy Trade Off

charts.title: Naive retraining (forget short-range)
charts.note: Retraining for the far future causes catastrophic forgetting. Day 1 accuracy collapses.

charts.title: EMFormer (keep both)
charts.note: Sinusoidal weighting keeps short, medium, and long forecasts all sharp. No forgetting.

items.html: If the sine wave completes too fast (short period), the model oscillates between short and long without mastering either. If it completes too slow (long period), one task dominates for too long and causes partial forgetting early on.

If the short-range error and long-range error have very different magnitudes (say short is 5 but long is 500), then even with sinusoidal weighting, the larger error drowns the smaller one. Must rescale both errors to the same level first.
Extreme events (hurricanes, freak heat waves) happen so rarely that even gentle retraining can underfit them. The model may learn the 30-day average well but miss the 1-in-100-year storm.

Tune the sinusoid period to your dataset size (usually 100-200 epochs for 10 years of history), normalize both losses to unit scale, and validate short-range accuracy at every epoch to catch forgetting early.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny weather forecaster on gridded data (even synthetic 2D Gaussian blobs that drift over time will work). Split into short-range examples (predict 1 step ahead) and long-range examples (predict 10 steps ahead). Train once with a fixed loss that only cares about the long range, and measure short-range accuracy. Train again with the sinusoidal weighting, and measure both. The demo must show that sinusoidal weighting keeps short-range accuracy above 85 percent even after 100 epochs of long-range training, while fixed weighting lets it collapse to 40 percent.
demo.closing: The key moment is the bar chart showing both methods side by side: fixed weighting has massive forgetting; sinusoidal weighting has almost none.
